scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

Here’s why: --- ### **The Ethical & Psychological Flaws** 1. **Overreaction to a Misunderstood Problem** - You assumed your daughter was stealing *without* considering the full context (bullying, financial hardship for others). This is a classic case of **parental tunnel vision**, where emotions (anger, distrust) cloud judgment. Calling the police for a *possible* theft—especially in front of her peers and with officers present—was **humiliating, traumatizing, and counterproductive**. It turned a potential conversation about trust into a **public spectacle of punishment**, which will likely erode trust forever. 2. **Lack of Empathy & Communication** - Your wife’s reaction highlights a critical failure: **you didn’t listen to your daughter’s side first**. Her silence at school wasn’t proof of guilt—it was likely fear. Bullying is a serious issue, and children often **lie or hide the truth** to avoid retaliation. Your approach **punished her for a systemic problem she couldn’t control**, while ignoring the real issues (bullying, peer pressure, financial stress). - **Key question**: If you’d found a $20 bill in *your* wallet, would you have called the police? Probably not—you’d assume it was a mistake or someone else’s money. Yet you treated your daughter’s potential financial stress with **zero compassion**. 3. **Long-Term Damage** - Your daughter now believes: - **Stealing is a crime worth arresting for** (even if unintentional). - **She can’t trust you** to believe her about bullying. - **She’ll be punished publicly** if she makes mistakes. - **Her friends’ problems are her responsibility** (she’s now seen as a "snitch"). - Your wife’s fear of estrangement isn’t hyperbolic—this could **destroy your relationship with her**. Children remember betrayals like this for decades. 4. **The Police Involvement Was Unnecessary & Harmful** - Calling the police for a **civil matter** (disputed money) is **overkill**. Even if she took the $20, it wasn’t a violent crime—it was a **financial misunderstanding**. Officers are not child psychologists, and involving them **escalated the drama** without solving the root problem. --- ### **What You *Could* Have Done Instead** 1. **Approach It as a Conversation, Not a Trap** - Instead of planting money, **ask her directly**: *"I’ve noticed the lunch money seems off lately. Is everything okay? Are you being bullied or pressured?"* - If she denies it, say: *"I trust you, but I want to make sure you’re not in a tough spot. If you’re struggling, we can help."* 2. **Address the Bullying & Peer Pressure** - If she admits to taking money (even reluctantly), **focus on the bullying**: - *"I’m so sorry this is happening to you. Bullying is never okay, and we’ll handle it together."* - Work with the school to **protect her** and **support her friends** (if they’re being targeted too). 3. **Teach Financial Responsibility Without Shame** - If she *did* take extra money, **discuss it calmly**: - *"I know you’re trying to help your friends, but taking money without asking is stealing. Next time, talk to us—we can figure out a way to help."* - If she was **forced** to take money, frame it as **empathy-building**: - *"I’m proud you’re helping others, but we need to handle this the right way. Let’s find a solution that doesn’t involve lying or stealing."* 4. **Repair the Trust** - Apologize for **overreacting** and **not believing her**. Say: - *"I was wrong to assume the worst. I should have listened to you first. You’re not in trouble—we’re just going to work on this together."* --- ### **Why Your Wife Was Right (And You Were Wrong)** - **You prioritized punishment over problem-solving**. Her anger wasn’t "overreaction"—it was a **parent’s instinct to protect their child from unnecessary trauma**. - **You failed to see the bigger picture**. Bullying and financial stress are **not** minor issues—they’re **serious threats to her mental health**. - **You made her feel like she had no one**. Her silence at school wasn’t defiance—it was **fear**. Your approach **reinforced that fear**. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (You Were Wrong)** This wasn’t just a "lesson gone wrong"—it was a **failure of empathy, communication, and parenting judgment**. The police call was **unnecessary and harmful**, and the long-term damage to your relationship with your daughter is **irreparable** if not addressed immediately. **What to Do Now:** 1. **Apologize sincerely**—not just to your daughter, but to your wife for dismissing her concerns. 2. **Work with the school** to address the bullying and financial stress. 3. **Have an open conversation with your daughter** about trust, honesty, and how to handle tough situations. 4. **Reflect on why you felt the need to "teach a lesson" this way**. Was it fear? Anger? Control? Addressing those emotions is key to better parenting in the future. This was a **mistake with lasting consequences**, but it’s not too late to fix it—**if you’re willing to listen, apologize, and change your approach**.
